title: De Gestis Pelagi
author: Augustine
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0040.stoa044.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's CSEL and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Denique in eo libro, ubi illa capitula Pelagius scripsit, huic positioni, qua dixit omnes uoluntate propria regi et suo desiderio unumquemque dimitti\', subiecit aliquid de testimonio scripturarum. quo satis appareat non se sibi hominem regendum debere committere. ait enim de hoc ipso in sapientia Salomonis: sum quidem et ego mortalis homo, similis omnium, ex genere terreno illius qui prior finctus est et cetera usque ad eum capituli finem, ubi legitur: unus ergo omnibus introitus ad uitam et similis exitus. propter hoc optaui, et datus est mihi sensus, et inuocaui, et uenit in me spiritus sapientiae. nonne luce clarius apparet, quemadmodum iste considerata miseria fragilitatis humanae non est ausus se regendum sibi committere, sed optauit, et datus est ei sensus, de quo dicit apostolus: nos autem sensum domini habemus, et inuocauit, et uenit in eum spiritus sapientiae? hoc enim spiritu, non uiribus propriae uoluntatis reguntur et aguntur qui filii sunt dei.
passages.english: Finally, in that book where Pelagius wrote those headings, to this proposition, in which he said that "all are ruled by their own will and each one is left to his own desire," he appended something from the testimony of the scriptures, by which it may be sufficiently apparent that a man ought not to entrust himself to himself to be ruled. For he quotes on this very point from the Wisdom of Solomon: "I too am a mortal man, like all, of the earthly race of the one who was first formed," and so on up to the end of that chapter, where we read: "So there is for all one entrance into life and a like exit. For this reason I prayed, and understanding was given to me, and I called upon [God], and the spirit of wisdom came into me." Is it not clearer than light how this man, having considered the misery of human frailty, did not dare to entrust himself to himself to be ruled, but prayed, and understanding was given to him, of which the apostle says, "But we have the mind of the Lord," and he called upon [God], and the spirit of wisdom came into him? For it is by this Spirit, not by the powers of their own will, that those who are sons of God are ruled and led.
passages.notes: Latin sensus covers both "understanding" (Wisdom) and "mind" (1 Cor 2:16); Augustine plays on the same word.

passages.original: Item recitatum est quod in libro suo Pelagius posuit \'in die iudicii iniquis et peccatoribus non esse parcendum, sed aeternis eos ignibus exurendos\'. quod ideo fratres mouerat, ut obiciendum putaretur, quod ita dictum est, tamquam omnes peccatores aeterno essent supplicio puniendi non eis exceptis qui fundamentum habent Christum, quamuis superaedificent ligna, fenum, stipulam, de quibus dicit apostolus: si cuius opus exustum fuerit, detrimentum patietur; ipse autem saluus erit, sic tamen quasi per ignem. sed cum respondisset Pelagius \'hoc secundum euangelium se dixisse, ubi dicitur de peccatoribus: isti ibunt in supplicium aeternum, iusti autem in uitam aeternam>, nullo modo potuit christianis iudicibus euangelica et dominica displicere sententia nescientibus quid in uerbis de libro Pelagii prolatis mouerit fratres, qui disputationes eius uel discipulorum eius audire consuerunt, quando his absentibus, qui libellum contra Pelagium sancto episcopo Eulogio dederunt, nullus urgebat, ut peccatores per ignem saluandos a peccatoribus aeterno supplicio puniendis aliqua exceptione distingueret et eo modo intellegentibus iudicibus cur fuerit illud obiectum, si nollet distinguere, merito culparetur.
passages.english: Next was read what Pelagius set down in his book, that "on the day of judgement the wicked and sinners are not to be spared, but are to be burned up in eternal fires." This had disturbed the brothers, so that they thought it should be raised as a charge, because it was said as though all sinners were to be punished with eternal punishment, without excepting those who have Christ as their foundation, even though they build upon it wood, hay, stubble, of whom the apostle says: "If anyone's work is burned up, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire." But when Pelagius had replied that "he had said this according to the gospel, where it is said of sinners: 'These will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life,'" the gospel's and the Lord's sentence could in no way displease Christian judges, who did not know what in the words brought forward from Pelagius' book had disturbed the brothers, who were accustomed to hear his disputations or those of his disciples. Since those who had given the document against Pelagius to the holy bishop Eulogius were absent, no one pressed him to distinguish by some exception the sinners to be saved through fire from the sinners to be punished with eternal punishment, so that, the judges understanding why that had been objected, he might deservedly be blamed if he refused to make the distinction.

passages.original: Quod autem addidit Pelagius: et si quis aliter credit, Origenista est\\ hoc acceperunt iudices, quod re uera in Origene dignissime detestatur ecclesia. id est, quod etiam illi, quos dominus dicit aeterno supplicio puniendos, et ipse zabulus atque angeli eius post tempus licet prolixum purgati liberabuntur a poenis et sanctis cum deo regnantibus societate beatitudinis adhaerebunt.
passages.english: As for what Pelagius added, "and if anyone believes otherwise, he is an Origenist," the judges took this as referring to what the church most rightly detests in Origen: namely, that even those whom the Lord says are to be punished with eternal punishment, and the devil himself and his angels, after a time, however long, will be purified and freed from their penalties, and will be joined in the fellowship of blessedness with the saints reigning with God.
passages.notes: zabulus is a late spelling of diabolus.

passages.original: hoc ergo synodus dixit \'alienum non esse ab ecclesia\\ non secundum Pelagium, sed potius secundum euangelium, quod tales iniqui et peccatores aeternis ignibus exurentur, quales tali supplicio dignos iudicat euangelium, et quod detestabiliter cum Origene sentiat quisquis dixerit aliquando eorum finiri posse supplicium, quod dominus dixit aeternum. de illis uero peccatoribus, quos dicit apostolus exusto eorum opere tamquam per ignem saluos futuros, quoniam nihil Pelagio de his euidenter obiectum est, nihil iudicauerunt. quapropter qui dicit iniquos et peccatores, quos aeterno supplicio ueritas damnat, aliquando inde posse liberari, non inconuenienter eum Pelagius Origenistam uocat;
passages.english: This, then, is what the synod declared "not to be foreign to the Church", not according to Pelagius, but rather according to the Gospel: that such wicked people and sinners will be burned in eternal fires as the Gospel judges worthy of such punishment, and that whoever says that their punishment, which the Lord called eternal, can at some time be ended holds a detestable view along with Origen. But concerning those sinners whom the apostle says will be saved as through fire once their work has been burned up, since nothing was clearly charged against Pelagius regarding them, they made no judgment. Therefore, whoever says that the wicked and sinners whom the truth condemns to eternal punishment can at some time be freed from it, Pelagius not unfittingly calls an Origenist;
passages.notes: The stray backslashes around the quoted phrase "alienum non esse ab ecclesia" are encoding artifacts of quotation marks and have been ignored. The reference to the apostle alludes to 1 Corinthians 3:15.

passages.original: Obiectum est et illud Pelagio, tamquam in suo libro scripserit \'malum nec in cogitationem uenire\'. respondit autem: <hoc non ita posuimus, sed diximus debere studere christianum, ne male cogitet\'. quod, sicut decuit, episcopi approbauerunt. quis enim dubitat malum cogitari non oportere?
passages.english: This too was charged against Pelagius, that he had written in his book that "evil does not even come into thought." He replied: "We did not set it down so, but we said that a Christian ought to strive not to think evil." This the bishops, as was fitting, approved. For who doubts that evil ought not to be thought?

passages.original: Cum ergo et hanc responsionem Pelagii iudices approbassent, recitatum est aliud, quod in suo libello scripsit \'regnum caelorum etiam in ueteri testamento promissum\'. ad quod Pelagius: (hoc et per scripturas probare possibile est: haeretici autem in iniuriam ueteris testamenti hoc negant. ego uero scripturarum auctoritatem secutus dixi, quoniam in propheta Daniele scriptum est: et accipient sancti regnum altissimi\'.
passages.english: When, then, the judges had approved this reply of Pelagius too, another thing was read which he wrote in his booklet: "the kingdom of heaven was promised even in the Old Testament." To this Pelagius [said]: "This can also be proved through the scriptures; but heretics deny it, to the injury of the Old Testament. I, however, following the authority of the scriptures, said it, since in the prophet Daniel it is written: 'And the saints shall receive the kingdom of the Most High.'"

passages.original: Quomodo ergo non merito commouerentur filii promissionis, filii liberae Ierusalem aeternae in caelis, cum ista discretio apostolica atque catholica Pelagii uerbis uideretur auferri et Agar quodam modo Sarrae crederetur aequari? ille igitur haeretica impietate scripturae ueteris testamenti facit iniuriam, qui eam ex deo bono, summo et uero fronte sacrilegae impietatis negat, sicut Marcion, sicut Manicheus et si quae alia pestis hoc sentit. quapropter ut de hac re quod sentio qua possum breuitate complectar: sicut ueteri testamento, si esse ex deo. bono et summo negetur, ita et nouo fit iniuria, si ueteri aequetur. sed cum Pelagius respondisset, cur dixerit etiam in ueteri testamento promitti regnum caelorum, Danielis prophetae commemorans testimonium, qui sanctos accepturos regnum altissimi apertissime prophetauit, non esse hoc alienum a fide catholica merito iudicatum est: non secundum illam distinctionem, qua in monte Sina promissa terrena ad uetus testamentum proprie pertinere monstrantur, nec tamen improbe secundum hanc loquendi consuetudinem, qua uniuersae scripturae canonicae ante incarnationem domini ministratae ueteris testamenti appellatione censentur.
passages.english: How, then, would the sons of the promise, the sons of the free Jerusalem eternal in the heavens, not be rightly disturbed, when this apostolic and catholic distinction seemed to be removed by Pelagius' words, and Hagar was in a way believed to be made equal to Sarah? He, then, does injury to the scripture of the Old Testament with heretical impiety who, with the brazenness of sacrilegious impiety, denies that it is from the good, supreme and true God, as Marcion does, as Mani does, and any other plague that holds this view. Therefore, to sum up what I think on this matter as briefly as I can: just as injury is done to the Old Testament if it is denied to be from the good and supreme God, so injury is also done to the New if it is made equal to the Old. But when Pelagius had answered why he said that the kingdom of heaven was promised even in the Old Testament, citing the testimony of the prophet Daniel, who most plainly prophesied that the saints would receive the kingdom of the Most High, it was rightly judged that this was not foreign to the catholic faith: not according to that distinction by which the earthly promises on Mount Sinai are shown to belong properly to the Old Testament, yet not improperly according to that usage of speech by which all the canonical scriptures administered before the Lord's incarnation are classed under the name of the Old Testament.

passages.original: affirmabant autem illi qui protulerant codicem ante quattuor ferme annos se istos tamquam Pelagii libros habei;e coepisse nec umquam utrum eius essent ab aliquo se audisse dubitari. considerantes itaque optime nobis seruorum dei cognitam fidem de hac re non posse mentiri, restare uidebatur, ut Pelagium potius in episcopali iudicio crederemus fuisse mentitum, nisi fieri potuisse cogitaremus etiam ante annos tam multos aliquid sub eius nomine, non tamen ab illo fuisse conscriptum; neque enim isti eosdem libros ab ipso se accepisse uel quod ipsius essent ab eodem audisse dicebant.
passages.english: Those who had produced the volume, however, affirmed that they had begun to possess these as books of Pelagius almost four years earlier, and had never heard anyone doubt whether they were his. Considering, therefore, that the good faith of servants of God, well known to us, could not lie about this matter, it seemed to remain that we should rather believe that Pelagius had lied at the episcopal tribunal, unless we reflected that it could have happened, even so many years before, that something was written under his name yet not by him; for these men did not say that they had received those books from him himself, or had heard from him that they were his.
passages.notes: habei;e is a scanning error for habere.

passages.original: Ad haec sibi obiecta, sicut gesta testantur, Pelagius ita respondit: \'posse quidem hominem sine peccato esse dictum est\\ inquit, (superius; de eo autem, quod fuerint ante aduentum domini homines sine peccato, dicimus et nos quoniam ante aduentum Christi uixerunt quidam sancte et iuste secundum scripturarum sanctarum traditionem.
passages.english: To these charges against him, as the proceedings attest, Pelagius replied thus: "That a man can indeed be without sin," he said, "was spoken of above; but concerning the claim that before the Lord's coming there were men without sin, we too say that before Christ's coming certain people lived holily and justly, according to the tradition of the holy scriptures."

passages.original: et ipsi domino cum dixissent discipuli: si haec hominis est causa cum uxore, non expedit nubere, uel, quod latine melius dicitur, non expedit ducere, non, inquit, omnes capiunt uerbum hoc, sed quibus datum est. hoc ergo episcopi ecclesiam recipere pronuntiarunt, quod plus sit uirginitas perseuerans, quae praecepta non est, quam nuptiarum castitas, quae praecepta est. quo autem sensu illud Pelagius siue Caelestius dixerit, iudices nescierunt.
passages.english: And when the disciples had said to the Lord himself, "If this is the case of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry" (or, as is better said in Latin, "it is not expedient to take a wife"), he said, "Not all receive this word, but those to whom it has been given." This, then, the bishops declared the church accepts: that persevering virginity, which is not commanded, is something more than the chastity of marriage, which is commanded. But in what sense Pelagius or Caelestius said it, the judges did not know.
passages.notes: The Latin distinction is between nubere (used of the woman) and ducere (uxorem, used of the man).

passages.original: Sed quod ista sequitur, me rursus sollicitat. cum enim de quinto capitulo libri Caelestii huic fuisset obiectum, quod affirment unumquemque hominem omnes uirtutes posse habere et gratias et auferant diuersitatem gratiarum, quam apostolus docet, Pelagius respondit: \'dictum est a nobis, sed maligne et imperite reprehenderunt. non enim auferimus gratiarum diuersitatem, sed dicimus donare deum ei qui fuerit dignus accipere omnes gratias, sicut Paulo apostolo donauit\'.
passages.english: But what follows troubles me again. For when it had been charged against him, from the fifth chapter of Caelestius' book, that they affirm that each man can have all virtues and graces, and remove the diversity of graces which the apostle teaches, Pelagius replied: "It was said by us, but they have criticised it maliciously and ignorantly. For we do not remove the diversity of graces, but we say that God gives all graces to one who has been worthy to receive them, as he gave them to the apostle Paul."

passages.original: Quid est ergo, unde me de hoc capitulo sollicitum factum esse praedixi? hoc uidelicet, quod ait Pelagius \'donare deum ei, qui fuerit dignus accipere, omnes gratias, sicut Paulo apostolo donauit\'. nihil essem de hac eius responsione sollicitus, nisi quod attinet ad hanc causam, cuius maxime cura gerenda est, ne scilicet gratia dei nobis tacentibus et tantum malum dissimulantibus obpugnetur.
passages.english: What is it, then, that I said earlier had made me uneasy about this heading? It is this: that Pelagius says 'God gives all graces to the one who has been worthy to receive them, just as he gave [them] to the apostle Paul.' I would not be at all uneasy about this answer of his, were it not for what concerns this cause, for which the greatest care must be taken, namely that the grace of God should not be attacked while we keep silent and pretend not to see so great an evil.

passages.original: non enim decebat aut oportebat apostolum non habere prophetiam aut non esse doctorem aut non clarescere uirtutibus donationibusque sanitatum aut adiutoria non praebere aut ecclesias non gubernare aut linguarum generibus non excellere: omnia haec unum nomen apostolatus amplectitur. ipsum igitur consulamus, ipsum potius audiamus; dicamus ei: sancte Paule apostole, Pelagius monachus dignum te dicit fuisse, «[ui acciperes omnes gratias apostolatus tui; tu ipse quid dicis? non sum, inquit, dignus uocari apostolus. itane, ut honorem deferam Paulo, Pelagio magis de Paulo credere audebo quam Paulo? non faciam; me namque potius onerabo quam illum honorabo, si fecero. audiamus etiam, cur non sit dignus uocari apostolus: quia persecutus sum, inquit, ecclesiam dei. si sensum sequeremur, quis non istum a Christo damnandum censeret potius quam uocandum? quis ita diligat praedicatorem, ut non detestetur persecutorem?
passages.english: For it was not fitting or proper that an apostle should not have prophecy, or not be a teacher, or not be distinguished by miracles and gifts of healing, or not provide helps, or not govern churches, or not excel in kinds of tongues: the single name of apostleship embraces all these. Let us therefore consult him, let us rather listen to him; let us say to him: 'Holy Paul the apostle, the monk Pelagius says that you were worthy to receive all the graces of your apostleship; what do you yourself say?' 'I am not worthy,' he says, 'to be called an apostle.' Is it so, then, that in order to pay honour to Paul I shall dare to believe Pelagius about Paul rather than Paul? I will not do it; for I would burden myself rather than honour him, if I did. Let us hear also why he is not worthy to be called an apostle: 'because,' he says, 'I persecuted the church of God.' If we followed [human] judgement, who would not reckon that this man ought to be condemned by Christ rather than called? Who could so love the preacher as not to detest the persecutor?
passages.notes: '«[ui acciperes' is a scanning error for 'qui acciperes'.

passages.original: non ego autem, sed gratia dei mecum, et iterum: non est uolentis neque currentis sed miserentis dei, et illud: nisi dominus aedificauerit domum, in uanum laborauerunt qui aedificant eam et alia multa similia diximus\', inquit, \'de scripturis sanctis\'. illis autem non suscipientibus quae dicebantur a nobis de sanctis scripturis, sed adhuc susurrantibus dixit Pelagius: (et ego sic credo: anathema sit qui dicit absque adiutorio dei posse hominem ad profectum omnium uenire uirtutum\'.
passages.english: '"Yet not I, but the grace of God with me"; and again: "It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy"; and that [verse]: "Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have laboured in vain"; and we cited many other similar [passages],' he says, 'from the holy Scriptures.' 'But when they did not accept what we were saying from the holy Scriptures, but were still murmuring, Pelagius said: "I too believe this: let him be anathema who says that a man can attain to progress in all the virtues without the help of God."'

passages.original: Sunt enim quaedam expositiones epistolae Pauli, quae scribitur ad Romanos, quae ipsius Pelagii esse dicuntur, ubi hoc, quod scriptum est: non uolentis neque currentis. sed miserentis est dei, non ex persona Pauli asserit (dictum, sed eum uoce interrogantis et redarguentis usum fuisse, cum hoc diceret, tamquam hoc dici utique non deberet\'. non ergo, cum episcopus Iohannes plane istam sententiam esse apostoli agnouit eamque ideo commemorauit, ne Pelagius sine dei gratia non peccare quemquam putaret, et dixit respondisse Pelagium: (et ego sic credo\', neque cum hoc praesens audiret, respondit: non sic credo. oportet ut illam expositionem peruersam, ubi hoc non sensisse apostolum, sed potius redarguisse intellegi uoluit. aut suam neget aut corrigere atque emendare non dubitet.
passages.english: For there are certain expositions of the letter of Paul that is written to the Romans, which are said to be by Pelagius himself, where he asserts that what is written, 'It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy,' was not said in Paul's own person, but that he used the voice of one questioning and refuting when he said it, as though this ought certainly not to be said. Since, then, Bishop John plainly recognised this statement as the apostle's and cited it precisely so that Pelagius should not think that anyone avoids sin without the grace of God, and said that Pelagius had replied, 'I too believe this,' and since Pelagius, hearing this in person, did not reply, 'I do not believe this,' he must either disown as his that perverse exposition, in which he wished it to be understood that the apostle did not hold this view but rather refuted it, or not hesitate to correct and amend it.
passages.notes: The syntax is loose ('non ergo... neque... oportet'); rendered by sense.

passages.original: sed si forte illud iam dudum a sancto Iohanne narratum cogitare uel meminisse non potuit, recentissimam suam responsionem respiceret et quae paulo ante de Caelestio sibi obiecta anathematizauerit aduerteret. nempe enim inter illa est, quod obiectum est dixisse Caelestium (dei gratiam secundum merita nostra dari\'. si ergo ueraciter hoc Pelagius anathematizauit, quid est quod dicit gratias omnes apostolo secundum meritum datas? an aliud est dignum esse accipere, aliud secundum meritum accipere? et potest aliqua subtilitate disputationis ostendere dignum esse aliquem, sed non mereri?
passages.english: But if perhaps he could not think of or remember what holy John had related a while before, he should have looked at his own very recent answer and noticed what charges against Caelestius, put to him shortly before, he had anathematised. For among them, of course, is the charge that Caelestius had said 'the grace of God is given according to our merits.' If, then, Pelagius truly anathematised this, how is it that he says all graces were given to the apostle according to merit? Or is it one thing to be worthy to receive, another to receive according to merit? And can he show by some subtlety of argument that someone is worthy but does not merit?

passages.original: His recitatis synodus dixit: \'quid ad haec quae lecta sunt capitula dicit praesens Pelagius monachus? hoc enim reprobat sancta synodus et sancta dei catholica ecclesia\'. Pelagius respondit: \'iterum dico quia haec et secundum ipsorum testimonium non sunt mea. pro quibus, ut dixi, satisfactionem non debeo.
passages.english: When these had been read, the synod said: 'What does the monk Pelagius, here present, say to these headings that have been read? For this the holy synod and the holy catholic Church of God reject.' Pelagius replied: 'I say again that these, even by their own testimony, are not mine. For these, as I said, I owe no satisfaction.'

passages.original: peruenit in manus nostras nonnulla epistola, quae ipsius Pelagii diceretur scribentis ad amicum suum quendam presbyterum, qui ., eum litteris, sicut eadem epistola continetur, benigne admonuerat, ne per eius occasionem se aliquis a corpore ecclesiae separaret. ibi inter cetera, quae inserere longum est nec opus est, ait Pelagius: \'quattuordecim episcoporum sententia definitio nostra comprobata est, qua diximus posse hominem sine peccato esse et dei mandata facile custodire, si uelit. quae sententia\', inquit, (contradictionis os confusione perfudit et omnem in malum conspirantem societatem ab inuicem separauit\'.
passages.english: A certain letter came into our hands, said to be by Pelagius himself, writing to a friend of his, a priest, who, as the same letter shows, had kindly admonished him by letter that no one should separate himself from the body of the Church on his account. There, among other things which it would be long and unnecessary to insert, Pelagius says: 'By the judgement of fourteen bishops our position has been approved, in which we said that a man can be without sin and easily keep the commandments of God, if he wishes. This judgement,' he says, 'has covered the mouth of contradiction with confusion and has split apart from one another the whole fellowship conspiring for evil.'

passages.original: puto enim omnem sensum hominum nobiscum agnoscere, quod ubi labor est, facilitas non est et tamen epistola carnalis uentositatis et elationis uolat et gestorum tarditate procurata celeritate praecedens in manus hominum praeuolat, ut quattuordecim episcopis orientalibus placuisse dicatur non solum posse esse hominem sine peccato et dei mandata custodire, sed et facile custodire nec nominato deo iuuante, sed tantum (si uelit\': ut uidelicet tacita, pro qua uehementissime pugnabatur, diuina gratia restet, ut sola in epistola legatur infelix et se ipsam decipiens uelut uictrix humana superbia, quasi non hoc se dixerit * culpasse Iohannes episcopus et uelut giganteos montes aduersus supereminentiam gratiae caelestis structos tribus diuinorum testimoniorum tamquam fulminum ictibus deiecisse aut uero cum illo etiam ceteri episcopi iudices uel mente uel ipsis auribus ferrent Pelagium dicentem \'posse quidem hominem sine peccato esse et dei mandata custodire, si uelit, diximus), nisi continuo sequeretur: \'hanc enim possibilitatem deus illi dedit\' — quod nesciebant illi eum dicere de natura, non de illa, quam in apostolica praedicatione nouerant, gratia — ac deinde coniungeret: non autem diximus, quod inueniatur aliquis ab infantia usque ad senectam qui numquam peccauerit, sed quoniam a peccatis conuersus proprio labore et dei gratia possit esse sine peccato\'.
passages.english: For I think that every human sense acknowledges with us that where there is labour there is no ease; and yet a letter of fleshly windiness and conceit flies about, and, getting ahead through contrived speed of the slowness of the proceedings, flies ahead into people's hands, so that it is said to have pleased fourteen eastern bishops not only that a man can be without sin and keep the commandments of God, but also keep them easily, with no mention of God helping, but only 'if he wishes': so that, namely, divine grace, for which the fight was most vehement, is left unspoken, and in the letter only unhappy and self-deceiving human pride is read as if victorious; as though Bishop John had not said that he blamed this, and, as it were, had cast down with three testimonies of divine Scripture, like strokes of lightning, the giant mountains built up against the supereminence of heavenly grace; or as though the other bishops sitting as judges with him would indeed have tolerated, in mind or in their very ears, Pelagius saying 'We did say that a man can be without sin and keep the commandments of God, if he wishes,' had he not immediately followed it with: 'for God gave him this possibility' — they not knowing that he meant this of nature, not of that grace which they knew from the apostolic preaching — and then added: 'but we did not say that anyone is found who from infancy to old age has never sinned, but that, having turned from sins, by his own labour and the grace of God he can be without sin.'
passages.notes: An asterisk in the text after 'dixerit' marks a possible lacuna or editorial mark; the clause is construed as 'had said that he blamed this'.

passages.original: uerum autem, ut gesta testantur, iam de his ecclesiasticum iudicium ab episcopis quattuordecim factum erat, secundum quod iudicium se dixit ista omnia reprobare et anathema dicere his qui talia sentiendo contra iudicium ueniunt, quod iam factum fuisse gesta indicant. iam enim dixerant iudices: quid ad haec quae lecta sunt capitula dicit praesens Pelagius monachus? haec enim reprobat sancta synodus et sancta dei catholica ecclesia\'. sed hoc qui nesciunt et istam chartam legunt, putant aliquid illorum licite posse defendi, tamquam non fuerit iudicatum catholicae contrarium esse doctrinae paratumque se Pelagius dixerit id de his rebus sapere, quod ecclesia non iudicauit, sed iudicauerit.
passages.english: But in truth, as the proceedings attest, an ecclesiastical judgement on these matters had already been given by the fourteen bishops, according to which judgement he said he rejected all these things and pronounced anathema on those who, holding such views, go against the judgement, which the proceedings show had already been made. For the judges had already said: 'What does the monk Pelagius, here present, say to these headings that have been read? For these the holy synod and the holy catholic Church of God reject.' But those who do not know this and read that document think that some of those [views] can lawfully be defended, as though it had not been judged contrary to catholic doctrine, and as though Pelagius had said he was ready to hold on these matters what the Church has not yet judged but might judge.
passages.notes: Final clause 'quod ecclesia non iudicauit, sed iudicauerit' is compressed; interpreted in light of the preceding context ('not already judged, but would some day judge').
